
## Polyenes · mechanism of action

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
- Amphotericin B is an amphipathic polyene macrolide from *Streptomyces nodosus*: a conjugated heptaene
  chromophore, a polyhydroxylated macrolactone ring, and a mycosamine aminosugar.
- Four mechanisms have been proposed — pore formation, oxidative damage, surface adsorption, and the
  **sterol sponge** model, in which large extramembranous aggregates *extract* ergosterol from the bilayer.
- The sterol sponge is now the best-supported account: killing correlates with simple ergosterol binding
  rather than with channel formation [@gray2012ampbsterol; @anderson2014spongeamb].
- Consequences that matter clinically: killing is **rapid and independent of fungal growth rate** (the target
  is pre-formed, no metabolic activation is needed), and resistance requires remodelling of the sterol
  pathway itself.
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.keypoint}
**One drug, four formulations.** The active moiety is identical; formulation changes distribution and
toxicity, **never spectrum**:

- amphotericin B deoxycholate (ABD, 1959)
- amphotericin B colloidal dispersion (ABCD)
- amphotericin B lipid complex (ABLC)
- liposomal amphotericin B (L-AmB)
:::

::: {.caution}
**Compounding traps for ABD.** Reconstitute in water or dextrose only — electrolyte-containing diluents
aggregate the colloid (visible clouding). A 0.22 µm in-line filter removes a substantial fraction of drug.
:::
:::
:::

## Polyenes · microbiology and spectrum

| Organism | Typical MIC~90~ (mg/L) | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| *C. albicans*, *C. tropicalis*, *C. parapsilosis* | 0.25–1 | Wild-type; EUCAST/CLSI susceptible ≤1 |
| *N. glabratus* (*C. glabrata*) | 0.5–1 | Reliably active; MICs slightly higher than *C. albicans* |
| *C. auris* | 1–>2 | **Amphotericin B resistance in ~30–40% of isolates** |
| *C. lusitaniae* | variable, often >1 | Classic intrinsic/inducible resistance |
| *Cryptococcus neoformans* | 0.25–1 | Backbone of induction therapy |
| *A. fumigatus* | 0.5–2 | Active; *A. terreus*, *A. lentulus*, *A. calidoustus* intrinsically resistant |
| Mucorales | 0.25–1 | Drug of choice for first-line therapy |
| *Fusarium* spp. | 1–>8 | Variable; *F. solani* complex least susceptible |
| *Scedosporium* / *L. prolificans* | >8 | Intrinsically resistant |

::: {.pearl}
**Where amphotericin B fails on the plate.** Primary resistance clusters in *A. terreus*, *A. calidoustus*,
*A. lentulus*, *Scedosporium*, *Trichosporon*, and — among yeasts — *C. lusitaniae* and *C. auris*. Acquired
resistance in normally susceptible species is rare and usually accompanied by reduced growth and virulence,
reflecting the cost of rebuilding the sterol pathway (*ERG2*, *ERG3* lesions, alternative sterols,
sphingolipid modulation).
:::

## Polyenes · ADME

| Parameter | Amphotericin B deoxycholate | Liposomal amphotericin B |
|---|---|---|
| **Absorption** | Not orally bioavailable; IV only | IV only (oral encochleated formulation investigational) |
| **Protein binding** | >95%, principally to β-lipoprotein | High; drug remains liposome-associated in circulation |
| **C~max~** | 0.5–2.0 mg/L at conventional doses, falling to a 0.2–0.5 mg/L plateau | Markedly higher C~max~ and AUC at equal mg/kg — up to ~10-fold [@groll2019lamb] |
| **Distribution** | Leaves plasma rapidly, binds cholesterol-containing membranes; stored in liver and other organs; localises to endothelium, including activated endothelium at infection sites | Preferential uptake by the reticuloendothelial system; high liver/spleen concentrations |
| **Metabolism / elimination** | Degraded *in situ*; only a small fraction excreted in urine or bile | Similar; negligible renal clearance of active drug |
| **Half-life** | Initial ~24 h; terminal β-phase ~15 days; detectable in serum up to 7 weeks after the last dose | Prolonged; supports intermittent high-dose strategies |
| **Organ dysfunction** | Blood levels **unaffected** by renal or hepatic failure; **not removed by haemodialysis** | No dose adjustment for renal replacement therapy |

::: {.source}
Formulation pharmacokinetics compiled from refs [@bellmann2017ampk; @hamill2013lamb; @groll2019lamb].
:::

## Polyenes · penetration into privileged sites

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="56%"}
- **CSF and brain: poor**, whether or not the meninges are inflamed — yet amphotericin B remains the
  backbone of cryptococcal meningitis induction. Efficacy there is not explained by CSF concentrations.
- **Vitreous and aqueous humour: low.** In *inflamed* serosal compartments (pleura, peritoneum, joint,
  ocular fluids) concentrations are roughly **two-thirds of the trough serum level**.
- **Urine: concentrations approximate serum** — the only conventional agent besides fluconazole and
  flucytosine that reliably treats renal parenchymal and urinary *Candida* disease.
- **Saliva, bronchial secretions, pancreas, muscle, bone: poor.**
:::
::: {.column width="44%"}
::: {.keypoint}
**The cryptococcal paradox.** Amphotericin B achieves minimal CSF concentrations yet produces the fastest
rate of CSF sterilisation of any agent. Explanations include cidal activity against organisms in the
subarachnoid space at low concentrations, high meningeal and choroid-plexus tissue binding, and the
long tissue residence of drug. The practical lesson: **plasma or CSF concentration is a poor surrogate for
polyene effect.**
:::
:::
:::

## Polyenes · pharmacodynamics

- **Concentration-dependent killing.** Time–kill and murine models show that effect is best described by
  **C~max~/MIC**; onset is rapid and unrelated to growth rate [@andes2001pd].
- **Prolonged post-antifungal effect**, consistent with drug remaining bound to membrane sterols after free
  concentrations fall.
- Together these properties justify **large, infrequent dosing** of the liposomal formulation.

::: {.keypoint}
**Clinical proof of the PD logic.** In AMBITION-cm, a **single 10 mg/kg** dose of liposomal amphotericin B
plus 14 days of flucytosine and fluconazole was non-inferior to 7 days of daily amphotericin B deoxycholate
for HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis, with **less toxicity** [@jarvis2022ambition].
:::

::: {.caution}
**More is not always better.** In AmBiLoad, liposomal amphotericin B 10 mg/kg/day for invasive mould disease
produced no efficacy benefit over 3 mg/kg/day but more nephrotoxicity and hypokalaemia
[@cornely2007ambiload]. Front-loading works for a single sterilising dose, not as a chronic daily strategy.
:::

## Polyenes · toxicity

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Nephrotoxicity — the dose-limiting effect**

- Dose-dependent fall in GFR via direct **afferent arteriolar vasoconstriction**, reducing glomerular and
  tubular blood flow.
- Tubular wasting of **potassium, magnesium and bicarbonate**; reduced erythropoietin production.
- Azotaemia is usually reversible; **permanent loss of function tracks cumulative dose**, not the peak
  creatinine, and reflects tubular cell destruction and nephron loss.
- **Saline loading** (≈1 L before each ABD dose) reduces nephrotoxicity in some but not all studies; potassium
  and magnesium replacement is routinely needed.
- A rising creatinine to **2–3 mg/dL** is expected at therapeutic ABD doses and is not by itself a reason
  to stop.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Infusion-related reactions**

- Chills, fever and tachypnoea begin **30–45 min** after starting the first infusions, peak at 15–30 min,
  and settle over 2–4 h; attributed to proinflammatory cytokine release.
- Less common in young children and in patients on corticosteroids; milder with successive doses.
- Mitigation: paracetamol premedication, hydrocortisone 25–50 mg in the infusion, pethidine for established
  rigors.

**Other**

- Normocytic normochromic anaemia (haematocrit rarely <20–25%), nausea, anorexia, phlebitis.
- Rare: thrombocytopenia, arrhythmia, hepatic transaminase elevation, encephalopathy, seizures.
- **Lipid formulations reduce but do not abolish** nephrotoxicity and infusion reactions.
- **Virtually no CYP-mediated drug interactions** — but additive nephrotoxicity with calcineurin inhibitors
  and aminoglycosides.
:::
:::

::: {.source}
**TDM has no established role.** Routine measurement of serum, urine or CSF amphotericin B concentrations
does not aid management; monitoring is of renal function, potassium and magnesium.
:::

## Polyenes · clinical use

| Indication | Role |
|---|---|
| **Mucormycosis** | First-line therapy, liposomal formulation, high dose [@cornely2019mucormycosis] |
| **Cryptococcal meningitis** | Induction backbone with flucytosine; single-dose 10 mg/kg L-AmB regimen in resource-limited settings [@jarvis2022ambition; @molloy2018acta] |
| **Invasive candidiasis** | Alternative to echinocandins; preferred where CNS, ocular or urinary involvement is suspected [@pappas2016idsacandida] |
| **Invasive aspergillosis** | Second-line, or first-line when azole resistance is likely or azoles cannot be used [@patterson2016idsaaspergillosis; @ullmann2018escmidaspergillosis] |
| **Endemic mycoses** | Severe/disseminated disease induction, followed by oral triazole step-down |
| **Empirical therapy in persistent neutropenic fever** | Historical standard; largely replaced by pre-emptive, diagnostic-driven strategies |

::: {.pearl}
Choose the **lipid formulation** for essentially all systemic indications in high-income settings. Deoxycholate
retains a role where cost dominates and renal monitoring is feasible — and the single-dose liposomal regimen
now offers a toxicity-sparing alternative in exactly those settings [@jarvis2022ambition].
:::
